course.title: Climate Science & Sustainability
course.description: An evidence-based introduction to how Earth's climate works and how societies can use energy, water, and land more sustainably — from the greenhouse effect to renewable energy and personal footprints. Structure adapted from OpenStax environmental and Earth science materials (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: The greenhouse effect is best described as…
options: sunlight being blocked before it reaches Earth
certain gases trapping outgoing heat and warming the surface
the ozone hole letting in extra heat
pollution physically heating the air by friction
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared (heat) radiation, keeping the surface warmer — see 'The greenhouse effect and the carbon cycle'.

questions.prompt: Which gas is the main long-lived driver of human-caused warming?
questions.explanation: CO₂ from burning fossil fuels is the dominant long-lived greenhouse gas — covered in 'The greenhouse effect'.

questions.prompt: Most of the extra heat trapped by the climate system ends up in the…
questions.explanation: Over 90% of the added energy is stored in the oceans — see 'Evidence for climate change'.

questions.prompt: Fossil fuels are called 'fossil' because they…
options: formed from ancient buried organic matter over millions of years
are dug up like fossils by geologists
questions.explanation: Coal, oil, and gas are carbon from ancient organisms — see 'Energy systems'.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a renewable energy source?
questions.explanation: Solar is replenished continuously; fossil fuels are finite — see 'Energy systems'.

questions.prompt: An 'ecological footprint' measures…
options: the biologically productive land and sea needed to support consumption
the size of a national park
questions.explanation: It compares demand on nature to what ecosystems can regenerate — see 'Ecological footprints'.

questions.prompt: 'Mitigation' of climate change mainly means…
options: adapting to impacts we can't avoid
questions.explanation: Mitigation reduces the cause (emissions); adaptation manages the effects — see 'Solutions'.

questions.prompt: The carbon cycle describes how carbon…
options: moves between the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living things
questions.explanation: Carbon continuously cycles among reservoirs — see 'The carbon cycle'.

lessons.title: The greenhouse effect and the carbon cycle
lessons.grammar_note: Greenhouse gases trap outgoing heat, not incoming sunlight — keep that distinction all course.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how the greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable and how carbon moves through the climate system. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which gas is the main long-lived driver of warming?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface, which then radiates energy back out as *infrared* (heat). *Greenhouse gases* — mainly water vapor, carbon dioxide (CO₂), and methane (CH₄) — absorb some of that outgoing heat and re-emit it, keeping the surface about 33 °C warmer than it would otherwise be. That natural effect makes life possible. The *carbon cycle* moves carbon between the atmosphere, oceans, soils, rock, and living things. Burning fossil fuels adds carbon that was locked underground for millions of years, so CO₂ builds up faster than natural sinks remove it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Atmospheric CO₂ was near 280 parts per million (ppm) before industrialization and passed 420 ppm by the 2020s — roughly a 50% increase. Measured directly at Mauna Loa since 1958, the curve rises every year with a small seasonal wiggle: it dips in Northern Hemisphere summer when plants take up carbon, and rises in winter when they release it. The steady upward trend is the human signal; the wiggle is the biosphere breathing.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Does the greenhouse effect trap incoming sunlight or outgoing heat? (2) Name two major greenhouse gases besides water vapor. (3) Why does the Mauna Loa CO₂ curve wiggle each year? (4) Where was fossil carbon before we burned it? Answers: (1) outgoing heat; (2) CO₂ and methane; (3) seasonal plant growth and decay; (4) locked underground in coal, oil, and gas.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole — they're separate issues. Mistake: thinking a warmer greenhouse effect is 'unnatural' — the effect itself is natural; the concern is the *added* CO₂ speeding it up. Exit: (a) In what form does Earth radiate energy back to space? (b) What human activity most increases atmospheric CO₂? Answers: infrared/heat; burning fossil fuels.

lessons.title: Evidence for climate change
lessons.grammar_note: Weather is a single day; climate is the long-term average — don't mix them up.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the main independent lines of evidence that Earth's climate is warming. Warm-up: where does most of the trapped extra heat end up?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: No single thermometer proves climate change; the case rests on many *independent* measurements that agree. Surface temperatures have risen roughly 1.1 °C since the late 1800s. Oceans store over 90% of the added heat and have warmed measurably. Glaciers and ice sheets are losing mass, Arctic sea-ice area is shrinking, and sea level is rising from both melting ice and thermal expansion of warmer water. *Weather* is any single day; *climate* is the decades-long average — a cold week doesn't undo a warming trend, just as one hot day doesn't prove it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Consider four unrelated datasets: (1) global surface temperature, (2) ocean heat content, (3) satellite-measured ice mass, (4) tide-gauge sea level. Each is collected by different instruments and teams, yet all point the same direction over decades. When independent methods converge, confidence is high — that convergence is why scientific bodies describe the warming trend as well established, while still quantifying uncertainty in the exact numbers.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Is a single cold winter evidence against a warming climate? (2) Name two causes of rising sea level. (3) Roughly how much has global surface temperature risen since the late 1800s? (4) Why is agreement among independent datasets persuasive? Answers: (1) no — that's weather, not the long-term trend; (2) melting land ice and thermal expansion; (3) about 1.1 °C; (4) independent methods are unlikely to share the same error.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating one extreme weather event as proof or disproof — trends need many years of data. Mistake: assuming the whole ocean has warmed uniformly (it hasn't; the surface and upper layers warm fastest). Exit: (a) What's the difference between weather and climate? (b) Name one line of evidence besides air temperature. Answers: weather is short-term, climate is the long-term average; ocean heat, ice loss, or sea-level rise.

lessons.title: Energy systems: fossil fuels vs renewables
lessons.grammar_note: Energy (what we want) vs. emissions (a side effect) — a source can be judged on both.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compare how fossil fuels and renewables produce energy and why their emissions differ. Warm-up: why are coal, oil, and gas called 'fossil' fuels?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Most modern energy comes from *fossil fuels* — coal, oil, and natural gas — formed from ancient organic matter. Burning them releases stored energy and CO₂. *Renewables* such as solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal draw on flows that replenish continuously and emit little or no CO₂ while operating. Each source has trade-offs: fossil fuels are energy-dense and dispatchable but finite and carbon-emitting; solar and wind are clean and increasingly cheap but *variable*, so grids pair them with storage, flexible demand, and other sources to keep supply steady.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Compare 'lifecycle' emissions per unit of electricity — grams of CO₂-equivalent per kilowatt-hour (gCO₂e/kWh), counting construction through operation. Coal is roughly 800–1000, natural gas about 400–500, while solar, wind, and nuclear typically fall in the low tens. Even after accounting for manufacturing panels or turbines, renewables emit an order of magnitude less per kilowatt-hour than coal. That ratio — not any single number — is the reasoning behind shifting the electricity mix.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Which emits more CO₂ per kWh, coal or wind? (2) What does 'variable' mean for solar and wind? (3) Name one way grids handle that variability. (4) Do renewables have zero lifecycle emissions? Answers: (1) coal, by roughly ten to fifty times; (2) output rises and falls with sun and wind; (3) storage, flexible demand, or backup generation; (4) no — low but not zero, mainly from manufacturing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming renewables are useless because they're intermittent — a diverse grid with storage smooths this out. Mistake: assuming natural gas is 'clean' — it emits less CO₂ than coal but is still a fossil fuel. Exit: (a) Rank coal, gas, and wind by CO₂ per kWh, highest first. (b) What replenishes a renewable source? Answers: coal > gas > wind; a continuous natural flow like sunlight or wind.

questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing heat.

questions.prompt: Pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ was closest to…
questions.explanation: About 280 ppm before industrialization, now above 420.

questions.prompt: Most of the extra heat in the climate system is stored in the…
questions.explanation: Oceans hold over 90% of the added energy.

questions.explanation: Climate is the long-term average, not one week.

lessons.title: Water, food, and resource sustainability
lessons.grammar_note: Sustainable use means the rate of use stays at or below the rate of renewal.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what makes water, food, and material use sustainable or unsustainable. Warm-up: in one phrase, what does 'sustainable' mean for a resource?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A resource is used *sustainably* when we take it no faster than it renews. Freshwater is renewed by the water cycle, but *aquifers* — underground stores — recharge slowly, so pumping them faster than they refill lowers water tables. Food production depends on soil, water, and nutrients; practices that preserve soil and cut waste stretch those resources. Roughly a third of food produced is lost or wasted, so reducing waste is one of the largest low-cost levers. A *circular* approach — reuse and recycling — keeps materials in use instead of discarding them after one pass.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose an aquifer recharges at 100 million liters per year and a region pumps 130 million. Each year the deficit is 30 million liters, so the store falls steadily — this is 'groundwater mining,' unsustainable by definition even though water still flows from the tap today. The fix isn't a single act but closing the gap: use less, recharge more, or both, until withdrawal is at or below 100 million.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Is pumping an aquifer at 130% of its recharge rate sustainable? (2) Roughly what share of food is lost or wasted globally? (3) Name one benefit of a circular (reuse/recycle) approach. (4) What renews surface freshwater? Answers: (1) no — withdrawal exceeds renewal; (2) about a third; (3) it reduces demand for new raw materials and waste; (4) the water cycle.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming water is unlimited because it's renewable — renewal has a rate, and aquifers recharge slowly. Mistake: thinking recycling alone solves resource strain; reducing and reusing usually save more. Exit: (a) When is resource use sustainable? (b) Name one way to make food systems more sustainable. Answers: when use ≤ renewal rate; cutting waste, protecting soil, or eating lower-footprint foods.

lessons.title: Solutions: mitigation, adaptation, policy, and action
lessons.grammar_note: Mitigation reduces the cause (emissions); adaptation manages the effects — both matter.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish mitigation from adaptation and identify solutions at policy and personal levels. Warm-up: which one — mitigation or adaptation — reduces emissions?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Responses fall into two complementary categories. *Mitigation* reduces greenhouse gas emissions — cleaner electricity, efficient buildings, electrified transport, and protecting forests that store carbon. *Adaptation* manages impacts we can't fully avoid — flood defenses, drought-tolerant crops, and heat-ready cities. Both are needed: mitigation limits how much change happens; adaptation handles what already arrives. *Policy* tools (carbon pricing, efficiency standards, research funding) shift whole systems, while *individual action* (transport choices, home energy, diet, and civic engagement) adds up and signals demand — most effective when it supports, rather than substitutes for, systemic change.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Classify four measures. A sea wall protecting a harbor: *adaptation* — it doesn't cut emissions, it manages impact. Replacing a coal plant with wind: *mitigation* — it lowers emissions. A carbon price: *policy* that drives mitigation across an economy. Switching a household to an electric heat pump: *individual mitigation* whose scale grows as millions do it. Notice the same goal — a stable climate — is approached from different levels at once.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each as mitigation or adaptation: (1) building flood barriers, (2) insulating homes to use less energy, (3) planting drought-resistant crops, (4) shifting a grid to solar and wind. Answers: (1) adaptation, (2) mitigation, (3) adaptation, (4) mitigation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating mitigation and adaptation as either/or — the evidence supports doing both. Mistake: assuming individual action is either pointless or sufficient on its own — it matters most alongside policy and infrastructure change. Exit: (a) Define mitigation in one line. (b) Give one example of adaptation. Answers: reducing greenhouse gas emissions; flood defenses, drought-tolerant crops, or heat-ready cities.

options: at or below the renewal rate
questions.explanation: Use must not exceed how fast the resource renews.

questions.prompt: Building a sea wall to protect a city is an example of…
questions.explanation: It manages an impact rather than cutting emissions.

questions.prompt: Replacing a coal plant with wind power is mainly…
questions.explanation: It reduces emissions — mitigation.

questions.explanation: Roughly a third, making waste reduction a major lever.

lessons.title: Applied project: estimate and reduce your own carbon footprint

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Estimate your personal carbon footprint across a few everyday categories, then propose realistic reductions. You won't need perfect data — you'll reason clearly from rough numbers, the way a scientist estimates before measuring precisely.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) List your main emission sources across four categories: transport, home energy, food, and goods/services. 2) Estimate each roughly (for example, weekly car or transit distance, home electricity or heating, how often you eat high-footprint foods like beef, major purchases or flights). 3) Rank the categories from largest to smallest so you know where the biggest lever is. 4) Propose two or three specific, realistic changes and estimate their effect. 5) Note one change that needs systemic support (for example, a cleaner electricity grid) rather than individual effort alone.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ You covered all four categories, not just the easy ones. ✔ Your estimates are quantitative and reasonable, even if rough. ✔ You targeted your largest source first rather than the most visible one. ✔ Your proposed changes are specific and realistic, not vague resolutions. ✔ You distinguished what you can change directly from what depends on policy or infrastructure. If all five are true, you've reasoned about sustainability like an analyst — honestly, quantitatively, and without over- or under-stating any single action.
